Passage – 1


The uprising of 1857, often regarded as the first large-scale challenge to British authority in India, is frequently narrated through the
actions of soldiers, princes, and political leaders. Yet such narratives risk overlooking the varied and significant roles played by women
during the conflict. While a few figures achieved historical prominence, the participation of women extended far beyond these well-known
individuals. Their involvement ranged from military leadership and political mobilization to logistical support and intelligence gathering,
suggesting that the rebellion also reshaped the social boundaries within which women acted.


One of the most widely recognized figures of the revolt is Rani Lakshmibai. When the British annexed Jhansi through the Doctrine of
Lapse, she refused to accept the loss of sovereignty. Contemporary narratives portray her organizing resistance, training soldiers, and
defending the city during the siege of Jhansi. Her eventual death in battle transformed her into a lasting symbol of resistance and courage
in Indian historical memory.


Equally significant was Begum Hazrat Mahal, who assumed leadership in Lucknow after the exile of Wajid Ali Shah. She proclaimed her
young son the ruler of Awadh and coordinated resistance against British authority. Through proclamations and political appeals, she
sought to unite different groups by highlighting the perceived injustices of colonial rule.


Other women also played visible leadership roles in the rebellion. Rani Avantibai Lodhi of Ramgarh mobilized local forces and organized
armed resistance in central India. Jhalkari Bai is remembered in oral traditions for disguising herself as Lakshmibai to mislead British
forces and allow the queen to escape. Similarly, Uda Devi fought in the battle of Sikandar Bagh near Lucknow and is believed to have killed
several British soldiers before being killed herself.


In addition to these prominent examples, many women participated in less visible but essential ways. Some acted as couriers who carried
messages between rebel groups across towns and villages. Others sheltered fighters, hid weapons, or provided food and medical care to
wounded soldiers. These activities were rarely documented in official records, yet they formed a crucial support system that sustained the
rebellion.


The involvement of women in 1857 therefore complicates the conventional image of the uprising as an exclusively male domain. Their
participation reveals that the rebellion also functioned as a moment in which established social expectations could be temporarily
reconfigured. By assuming roles that ranged from political leadership to everyday acts of support, women demonstrated forms of agency
that have only gradually received recognition in historical scholarship. The study of these contributions broadens our understanding of the
uprising as not only a military revolt but also a wider social upheaval involving diverse participants.

Passage – 2


The Hungarian folktale Pretty Maid Ibronka offers a compelling metaphor for the contemporary predicament of academic philosophy. In
the story, the young protagonist ties herself to the devil in order to uncover hidden truths. Similarly, modern philosophers often find
themselves bound to an intellectual tradition shaped by exclusivity, disciplinary hegemony, and the persistent myth of the solitary genius.
Although philosophy claims universal aspirations, its historical development has frequently marginalized diverse voices and perspectives.


One of the most pressing debates within the discipline concerns the expansion of the philosophical canon. Scholars such as Jay Garfield
have argued that restricting philosophical inquiry primarily to European texts is intellectually indefensible. Only recently have philosophy
departments begun to engage more seriously with women thinkers and non-Western traditions. Yet broadening the canon often requires
moving beyond conventional philosophical formats. Figures like Margaret Cavendish illustrate the rare case of a woman writing within
established philosophical structures, but her social status and educational privilege were exceptional. To recover a wider range of
perspectives, scholars must look beyond traditional treatises and engage with alternative forms of intellectual expression.


Religious and theological texts have already begun to receive renewed philosophical attention. The works of figures such as Teresa of
Ávila and Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz are now examined not solely as theological reflections but as sources of philosophical insight.
Similarly, Buddhist philosophers including Dignga and Ratnakrti are increasingly incorporated into philosophical curricula. However, even
these developments often remain confined to literate and elite traditions. Folklore offers a further and largely neglected resource for
philosophical inquiry.


Folklore has historically developed through oral transmission and collective authorship. Because it flourishes outside elite literary cultures,
it frequently preserves perspectives from groups otherwise excluded from formal intellectual institutions. Women, in particular, have
played a central role in preserving and transmitting folktales across generations. As a result, folklore provides access to ethical reflection,
metaphysical speculation, and social commentary embedded within narrative traditions.


These stories frequently present dilemmas that closely resemble philosophical thought experiments. Tales such as the Russian legend of
Ilya Muromets raise questions about moral obligations to community versus strangers, while Haitian narratives about Death challenge
assumptions about justice and mortality. In some cultures, folklore even functions as a normative framework guiding ethical reasoning
and social practices.


Recognizing folklore as a source of philosophical reflection also challenges prevailing methodological assumptions. Academic philosophy
has traditionally privileged formal argumentation, yet narrative and storytelling have long played a role in philosophical thought, from
Plato's dialogues to Nietzsche's parables. By engaging with folklore, philosophers may expand both the scope of their sources and the
methods through which philosophical insight is pursued. In doing so, the discipline may rediscover a more inclusive and imaginative form
of inquiry.


(451 words, Aeon Essays, edited)

India's recent release of the new National Accounts series, updating the base year from 2011-12 to 2022-23, has performed a curious
double-act on the nation's economic stage. On the one hand, it has revised the projected GDP growth for 2025-26 upward to 7.6%. On the
other, it has shrunk the absolute size of the economy by roughly 3.3%, bringing it down to approximately Rs.345.47 lakh crore. This
downward revision of the "denominator"-the nominal GDP-has profound implications for the government's fiscal arithmetic.


While the new series incorporates more accurate data sources, such as the Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises (ASUSE)
and GST returns, it also moves the goalposts for the much-vaunted "$5 trillion economy" target. With the absolute GDP value being lower
than previously estimated and the rupee facing persistent depreciation against the dollar, India is currently a $3.8 trillion economy. The
path to $5 trillion now looks steeper, requiring not just consistent growth but a stabilization of the currency that is currently hostage to
global energy shocks.


Furthermore, the fiscal deficit and debt-to-GDP targets-expressed as a percentage of the total economy-are now harder to hit. When the
denominator shrinks, the ratio swells. This "statistical sobering" suggests that while India remains the world's fastest-growing major
economy, the cushion of fiscal space is thinner than the government's rhetoric previously suggested. The challenge for policymakers in
2026 is no longer just "growth at any cost," but "growth within the constraints of accuracy."

Well, one, I think southerners speak in metaphor a lot. The southern vernacular is very metaphoric and that is one of the things that I kind
of go for in my writing, is to allow ordinary characters, ordinary people, to speak in metaphor. Because they do. They just don't know the
word metaphor. But they emotionally know what a metaphor is. So that's one thing. But I think I became a writer simply because, like any
other child, like many other children, I liked to read. I think the gift that led me to writing ironically was the way that girls are ignored. I wrote
with no concern of what anyone would think of it because I never thought anyone would think anything of it. When girls like to read and
they like to write, people think of them as nice girls, one less thing for your parents to worry about. You know, I love to say no one ever got
pregnant in the library that I know of, and so I wrote only for my own pleasure and interest. And that is what I think really planted that seed
for me. But when I got to Spelman College, when I was just a kid. I was 16, my parents sent me to college very young. When I got to
Spelman, I met a writer, and she was my teacher, and she said to me, what are you thinking about these days? I got ready to tell her, and
she said, No, don't tell me, write it down. And with that, she took me seriously, and she became my first audience. And because she took
me seriously, I was able to take myself seriously. And that is when I first started to think of myself as a writer. Also at Spelman College,
there were, unlike my experience in high school or what have you, there were so many different ways for a young girl, a young woman, to
be popular. You could be popular as a pretty girl, that was in pageants. You could be popular by being like a really assertive leader that
served on a student government association. There were so many things. Some girls were popular because they could sing so beautifully,
and they were always asked to sing at events. And then there was a girl who everyone knew because she was the one who knew how to
write.

Legislative Assembly of Kerala passed a resolution on 24.06.2024 to alter the name of the State of "Kerala" to "Keralam", which is as under:
"The name of our State is 'Keralam' in Malayalam Language. States were formed on the basis of language on the 1st day of November,
1956. The Kerala Piravi Day is also on the 1st day of November. Since the time of National Independence Struggle, there has been a strong
demand for the formation of United Kerala for the people speaking Malayalam language. But in the First Schedule to the Constitution the
name of our State is recorded as 'Kerala'. This Assembly unanimously appeal to the Central Government to take urgent steps as per Article
3 of the Constitution for modifying the name as 'Keralam'." Thereafter, Government of Kerala has requested Government of India to take
necessary steps to amend the First Schedule to the Constitution by altering the name of State of 'Kerala' as 'Keralam' as per article 3 of the
Constitution.

name of any State. Further proviso to article 3 states that no Bill for the purpose shall be introduced in either House of Parliament except
on the recommendation of the President and unless, where the proposal contained in the Bill affects the area, boundaries or name of any

of the States, the Bill has been referred by the President to the Legislature of that State for expressing its views thereon within such period

Euthanasia refers to the termination of life to relieve suffering, and the law distinguishes between active euthanasia, involving a positive
act to cause death, and passive euthanasia, involving withdrawal or withholding of life-sustaining treatment. While active euthanasia
remains impermissible, passive euthanasia has been recognised within a limited constitutional framework. The Supreme Court has held
that the right to life under Article 21 includes the right to die with dignity, particularly in cases where medical treatment merely prolongs
biological existence without any realistic prospect of recovery. In a recent judgment, the Court permitted the withdrawal of life-sustaining
treatment for a patient in a persistent vegetative state for over a decade, emphasising that such decisions are not about ending life, but
about avoiding artificial prolongation of suffering. However, the Court maintained a strict distinction: withdrawal of treatment allows the
disease to take its natural course, whereas active intervention to cause death remains unlawful. Thus, the legality of passive euthanasia
depends not merely on outcome (death), but on the nature of the act and intention behind it.


Where the patient is competent, refusal of treatment is treated as an exercise of autonomy, not euthanasia. In cases of incapacity,
decisions must be guided by advance directives (living wills) or, in their absence, by a determination of the patient's best interests,
supported by medical evaluation. The process must include safeguards such as review by independent medical boards to ensure that the
decision is neither arbitrary nor influenced by extraneous considerations. The Court has further emphasised that neither family consent
nor medical opinion alone is sufficient; legality arises from a structured decision-making process grounded in dignity, consent, and
procedural safeguards. Any deviation risks transforming a constitutionally protected withdrawal of treatment into an impermissible act.
Thus, the law draws a careful balance: it recognises dignity in death but insists that such dignity must be realised through regulated,
evidence-based, and ethically grounded processes, not subjective judgments or unilateral decisions.

Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act declares void every agreement that restrains a person from exercising a lawful profession, trade, or
business. The provision is often described as adopting an absolute rule, in contrast to jurisdictions that permit reasonable restraints.
However, this apparent rigidity is tempered not by broad exceptions, but by careful characterisation of the nature and effect of the
restriction.


The central inquiry is not merely whether a clause appears restrictive, but whether its practical effect is to restrain trade. A clause that
regulates the manner of performance during a subsisting contract-such as exclusivity obligations-does not ordinarily offend Section 27, as
it does not extinguish future economic freedom. In contrast, restrictions that operate after termination are viewed with suspicion, since
they directly limit an individual's capacity to earn a livelihood.

The statute recognises a narrow exception in the context of sale of goodwill, where limited restraints may be upheld. Outside this, courts
do not ordinarily engage in a general inquiry into reasonableness. However, parties may attempt to structure restrictions indirectly, through
devices such as penalty clauses, forfeiture provisions, or conditional payments. Where such arrangements, in substance, deter or prevent
engagement in a lawful trade, they fall within the mischief of Section 27, regardless of their formal framing.

trade secrets may be enforceable, provided they do not operate as a blanket prohibition on employment or business activity. The
distinction lies in whether the clause protects a legitimate interest without restraining trade, or whether it effectively compels economic
inactivity.

restraints, but also arrangements that achieve the same result indirectly. The ultimate test is whether the agreement, in its real effect,
curtails the individual's freedom to engage in lawful economic activity beyond the permissible limits recognised by law.

The Doctrine of Fixtures refers to a legal principle that determines whether a chattel (movable property) has become part of the land or
building to which it is attached, thereby transforming into immovable property. The doctrine of fixtures revolves around two primary
considerations: the mode of annexation and the purpose of annexation.


1. Mode of Annexation: method and degree of attachment of a chattel to the land or building.
Physical Attachment: If a chattel is affixed to the land or building in a manner that it cannot be removed without causing damage to either
the chattel or the property, it is generally considered a fixture.


Presumption of Intent: In cases where the mode of annexation involves substantial integration with the property, there is a presumption
that the intent was to make the chattel a permanent part of the property.
Temporary vs. Permanent Attachment: The law distinguishes between items that are temporarily attached and those intended for
permanent installation.


2. Purpose of Annexation
The purpose of annexation examines the reason behind attaching the chattel to the property.


Enhancement of Property: If the chattel is annexed to enhance the property's value or utility in a permanent manner, it is likely to be
deemed a fixture.


Personal Use: Conversely, if the chattel is attached for the temporary use or benefit of the property owner and can be removed without
significantly affecting the property, it may remain classified as personal property.


Intention of the Parties: If it can be demonstrated that the parties intended for the chattel to remain personal property, even though it is
physically attached to the property, this intention may prevail.


Legal Tests and Application of Doctrine of Fixtures


The determination of whether a chattel has become a fixture often involves a combination of the mode and purpose of annexation, along
with other relevant factors. Courts may apply various tests to assess these factors, including:


Degree of Annexation Test: The more securely and permanently a chattel is affixed, the more likely it is to be considered a fixture.


Purpose of Annexation Test: Whether the chattel was intended to improve the property's functionality or simply to serve a temporary need.

Intention of the Parties: The expressed or implied intentions of the parties, as evidenced by contractual terms, conduct and the nature of
the property use.

The Doctrine of Fixtures refers to a legal principle that determines whether a chattel (movable property) has become part of the land or
building to which it is attached, thereby transforming into immovable property. The doctrine of fixtures revolves around two primary
considerations: the mode of annexation and the purpose of annexation.


1. Mode of Annexation: method and degree of attachment of a chattel to the land or building.
Physical Attachment: If a chattel is affixed to the land or building in a manner that it cannot be removed without causing damage to either
the chattel or the property, it is generally considered a fixture.


Presumption of Intent: In cases where the mode of annexation involves substantial integration with the property, there is a presumption
that the intent was to make the chattel a permanent part of the property.
Temporary vs. Permanent Attachment: The law distinguishes between items that are temporarily attached and those intended for
permanent installation.


2. Purpose of Annexation
The purpose of annexation examines the reason behind attaching the chattel to the property.


Enhancement of Property: If the chattel is annexed to enhance the property's value or utility in a permanent manner, it is likely to be
deemed a fixture.


Personal Use: Conversely, if the chattel is attached for the temporary use or benefit of the property owner and can be removed without
significantly affecting the property, it may remain classified as personal property.


Intention of the Parties: If it can be demonstrated that the parties intended for the chattel to remain personal property, even though it is
physically attached to the property, this intention may prevail.


Legal Tests and Application of Doctrine of Fixtures


The determination of whether a chattel has become a fixture often involves a combination of the mode and purpose of annexation, along
with other relevant factors. Courts may apply various tests to assess these factors, including:


Degree of Annexation Test: The more securely and permanently a chattel is affixed, the more likely it is to be considered a fixture.


Purpose of Annexation Test: Whether the chattel was intended to improve the property's functionality or simply to serve a temporary need.

Intention of the Parties: The expressed or implied intentions of the parties, as evidenced by contractual terms, conduct and the nature of
the property use.

The doctrine of strict liability imposes responsibility on a person who, for their own purposes, brings onto their land and keeps anything
likely to cause harm if it escapes. If such a thing escapes and causes damage, liability arises regardless of negligence. However, this rule
is subject to several well-recognised exceptions, including acts of God, acts of third parties, plaintiff's own fault, consent, and statutory
authority.


A critical requirement under strict liability is "escape", meaning that the harmful substance must move from the defendant's control to a
place outside it. Further, the use of land must be non-natural, implying a special or extraordinary use that increases danger to others.


In contrast, the doctrine of absolute liability, developed in response to modern industrial hazards, imposes a more stringent standard.
Where an enterprise is engaged in inherently dangerous or hazardous activities and harm results, the enterprise is absolutely liable,
without any exceptions. The absence of negligence, or the presence of intervening factors such as third-party actions, does not absolve
liability.


Unlike strict liability, absolute liability does not require proof of escape in a narrow sense, nor does it permit defences based on
foreseeability or external interference. The rationale lies in the principle that enterprises engaged in hazardous activities owe a non-
delegable and absolute duty to the community, and must bear the cost of harm as part of their operational risk.


Thus, while strict liability balances risk with recognised defences, absolute liability reflects a policy shift toward enterprise accountability,
particularly where the magnitude of potential harm is significant. The distinction between the two doctrines depends not merely on the
occurrence of harm, but on the nature of the activity, the presence or absence of exceptions, and the extent to which liability is conditioned
or unconditional.

Trademark infringement arises when a registered trademark is used by another in a manner that is identical or deceptively similar, in
relation to goods or services covered by the registration, such that it is likely to cause confusion or association in the minds of the public.
The inquiry is not confined to actual confusion but extends to the likelihood of confusion, assessed from the perspective of an average
consumer with imperfect recollection.


A key principle is that infringement may occur even where the marks are not identical, provided the defendant's mark appropriates the
essential features of the registered mark. The comparison is based on overall impression rather than a meticulous side-by-side analysis.
Phonetic similarity, visual resemblance, and conceptual association may all be relevant.


The nature of goods and the class of consumers are also significant. Where goods are similar or allied, even a moderate degree of

resemblance may suffice. Conversely, where goods are dissimilar, infringement may still arise if the registered mark has a strong
reputation and the use by another takes unfair advantage or is detrimental to its distinctive character-commonly referred to as dilution.


Defences to infringement are limited. Use of one's own name, descriptive use, or bona fide use indicating characteristics of goods may be
permissible, provided such use is honest and not calculated to deceive. However, mere addition of prefixes, suffixes, or disclaimers does
not avoid infringement if the dominant part of the mark remains deceptively similar.


Importantly, intention to deceive is not essential for infringement, though it may strengthen the inference of confusion. Similarly, absence
of actual damage does not preclude relief if likelihood of confusion is established.


Thus, trademark law protects not only against direct imitation but also against subtle forms of appropriation, ensuring that the source-
identifying function of marks is not undermined by deceptive similarity or unfair association.

Bigamy arises when a person, having a living spouse, contracts another marriage during the subsistence of the first. The offence is
premised on the existence of a valid and legally recognised first marriage. If the first marriage is void or not legally established, the
question of bigamy does not arise.


A crucial requirement is that the first marriage must be subsisting at the time of the second marriage. If the first marriage has been
dissolved by a valid decree of divorce, or declared void by a competent court, a subsequent marriage does not attract liability. Similarly,
where the first spouse is presumed dead under law after prolonged absence, a second marriage may not amount to bigamy.


The validity of the second marriage is also relevant. If the alleged second marriage does not fulfil essential legal ceremonies or
requirements necessary to constitute a valid marriage under the applicable personal law, it may not be recognised as a "marriage" in law,
and consequently, the offence of bigamy may fail.


Conversion to another religion does not automatically dissolve an existing marriage. A person cannot evade liability for bigamy merely by
changing religion and contracting another marriage unless the first marriage has been legally terminated.


Proof plays a central role. The burden lies on the party alleging bigamy to establish both the validity of the first marriage and the fact of a
legally recognised second marriage. Mere cohabitation, social acknowledgment, or informal ceremonies may be insufficient unless they
satisfy legal requirements.


Thus, the offence of bigamy depends on a combination of factors: the existence of a valid and subsisting first marriage, the legal validity
of the second marriage, and compliance with evidentiary requirements. Without satisfying these elements, criminal liability cannot be
sustained.

current national accreditation system for public and private sector hospitals must be streamlined to ensure compliance. Stricter

Passage – 2


Edward Gibbon is one of 18th century Britain's other great prose stylists. The sentences of Gibbon that I love most come from his
memoirs, which exist in a host of drafts braided together for publication after his death. As a young man, Gibbon fell in love and asked
permission of his father to marry. But his spendthrift father had depleted the family's resources so much that he told Gibbon not to. 'I
sighed as a lover, I obeyed as a son,' Gibbon wrote. The aphoristic parallelism in that lovely sentence does some work of emotional self-
protection. Also from Gibbon's memoirs: 'It was at Rome, on the fifteenth of October 1764, as I sat musing amidst the ruins of the Capitol,
while the barefooted friars were singing vespers in the temple of Jupiter, that the idea of writing the decline and fall of the City first started
to my mind.' The precision of the place and time setting, the startling contrast effected by the juxtaposition of barefooted friars and the
pagan temple, the fact that there is an exterior soundscape as well as an internal thoughtscape, the way the sentence builds to the
magnitude of the project to come - all work to make the sentence great.


The first sentence of any novel works as an invitation into a new world. Sometimes that invitation is so powerful that the sentence itself
takes on a life of its own. One example: the opening sentence of Orwell's 1984: 'It was a bright cold day in April, and the clocks were
striking thirteen.' The sentence is initially unassuming, simply descriptive, but in the startling final detail Orwell achieves estrangement,
establishing the alternate nature of the novel's historical reality with economy and force. Another opening line from near-future speculative
fiction is that of William Gibson's debut novel Neuromancer: 'The sky above the port was the color of television, tuned to a dead channel.'
The startling metaphor seemed to speak with remarkable directness to a world in which new forms of media and mediation had come to
define human consciousness. The passage of time has raised questions, however. Today, to a generation of readers who barely watch TV
on 'channels' and don't really know what a 'dead' one would look like, the metaphor will be nearly inscrutable.

Edward Gibbon is one of 18th century Britain's other great prose stylists. The sentences of Gibbon that I love most come from his
memoirs, which exist in a host of drafts braided together for publication after his death. As a young man, Gibbon fell in love and asked
permission of his father to marry. But his spendthrift father had depleted the family's resources so much that he told Gibbon not to. 'I
sighed as a lover, I obeyed as a son,' Gibbon wrote. The aphoristic parallelism in that lovely sentence does some work of emotional self-
protection. Also from Gibbon's memoirs: 'It was at Rome, on the fifteenth of October 1764, as I sat musing amidst the ruins of the Capitol,
while the barefooted friars were singing vespers in the temple of Jupiter, that the idea of writing the decline and fall of the City first started
to my mind.' The precision of the place and time setting, the startling contrast effected by the juxtaposition of barefooted friars and the
pagan temple, the fact that there is an exterior soundscape as well as an internal thoughtscape, the way the sentence builds to the
magnitude of the project to come - all work to make the sentence great.


The first sentence of any novel works as an invitation into a new world. Sometimes that invitation is so powerful that the sentence itself
takes on a life of its own. One example: the opening sentence of Orwell's 1984: 'It was a bright cold day in April, and the clocks were
striking thirteen.' The sentence is initially unassuming, simply descriptive, but in the startling final detail Orwell achieves estrangement,
establishing the alternate nature of the novel's historical reality with economy and force. Another opening line from near-future speculative
fiction is that of William Gibson's debut novel Neuromancer: 'The sky above the port was the color of television, tuned to a dead channel.'
The startling metaphor seemed to speak with remarkable directness to a world in which new forms of media and mediation had come to
define human consciousness. The passage of time has raised questions, however. Today, to a generation of readers who barely watch TV
on 'channels' and don't really know what a 'dead' one would look like, the metaphor will be nearly inscrutable.

Source: Aeon Essays: The history of conceptual art is often traced back to the early 20th-century work of Marcel Duchamp, who presented
everyday objects like a snow shovel or a bottle rack as his own artworks, raising questions about the nature of art and proposing that
artistic creativity need not involve skilled fabrication. Hardedged conceptual art, which sometimes involved no material objects at all, had
its heyday in the 1960s and '70s, captured by the artist Sol LeWitt's statement in 1969 that 'Ideas alone can be works of art; they are in a
chain of development that may eventually find some form. All ideas need not be made physical.'


Subsequent decades have seen the proliferation of a movement of conceptual art more broadly construed in which the object, even if
sometimes carefully constructed and essential to the work, points beyond itself to an idea or conceptual framework that may not be
readily evident. When encountering the works I've described - all of which are real - we may experience increasing perplexity. What is going
on here? What should we do with these works? What values are they pursuing? Are they any good? Above all, how would we start on
getting answers to these questions?


The decline of traditional artistic media has helped to pull the rug out from under us. Artists have chipped away at, and sometimes
abandoned wholesale, the conventions and boundaries that previously oriented us. Take painting, a medium that was long governed by
conventions so obvious that it would have seemed silly to list them: a painting involves paint applied to a surface, presented so that the
representational content is the right side up and facing away from the wall. But artists have toyed with this model: Georg Baselitz makes
paintings whose content is to be presented upside down; Fiona Banner made a painting whose primary marked surface is displayed facing
the wall; Saburo Murakami made paintings whose paint was designed to flake away over time.


In many years of studying conceptually oriented works, both in the gallery and by way of files held in museums' back rooms, I began to
discern a shared structure that allows us to make sense of the artists' projects in relation to one another and to their historical precursors.
There is an underlying logic and set of constraints that constitute specific choices as meaningful. While the materiality of these works is
all over the place, they are bolstered by an immaterial scaffold: a set of rules that point us toward what the artist is up to and what really
matters.

The following information relates to the total number of trainees enrolled in yearly courses at four training institutes—A, B, C, and D—during
the years 2021 to 2024. Each institute offers training only in Programming, Design, and Data Analytics.


The total number of trainees enrolled in Institute A during the four years was 12,000, which was 75% of the total number enrolled in
Institute B. In Institute A, the number of trainees in 2024 was 35% of its four-year total, while the number of trainees in 2021 and 2023 was
the same. The total number of trainees in Institutes C and D during the four years was 20% less and 20% more than that in Institute A,
respectively. In the year 2022, the number of trainees admitted in each institute was 25% of the total trainees admitted in that institute
during the four years. In Institute B, the ratio of admissions in 2023 and 2024 was 25 : 14. Also, the number of admissions in 2021 was
200 more than that in 2022. In Institute C, the admissions in 2021 were 600 fewer than those in 2023. The admissions in 2024 were 1,200
more than those in 2023. In Institute D, the number of trainees admitted in 2021 and 2023 was the same, while the admissions in 2024
were 50% more than those in 2022.

A national health organization conducted a survey to understand the age-wise distribution of patients visiting government hospitals in a
large metropolitan region. The objective of the survey was to help healthcare authorities plan better medical facilities, specialized wards,
and preventive health programs for different age groups. The survey revealed that 26% of the patients visiting government hospitals are
children in the age group of 0-14 years. The next major group consists of young individuals aged 15-24 years, who account for 18.4% of
the total patients. Among the adult population seeking medical care, 16.8% belong to the 25-34 years age group, while 15.6% fall in the 35-
44 years category. Patients aged 45-54 years constitute 12.75% of the total. The proportion of older patients is relatively smaller.
Individuals aged 55-64 years account for 7.25%, whereas those aged 65 years and above represent only 3.2% of the total patients visiting
the hospitals. Consider the ages of the patients in integer years.
